phonemes.desc: Short alpha [a] — the neuter of πᾶς, 'all,' opening the name.
Long omega [ɔː] bearing the acute pitch — the stressed heart of the name, from δῶρον, 'gift.'
Short final alpha [a], light and open.

pronunciation.approximation: 'pan-DOH-rah' — the stress rides the long middle syllable; hold the 'o,' as befits the word 'gift.'

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Πανδώρα (Pandṓra), πᾶν 'all' + δῶρον 'gift' — 'All-gifted' (Hesiod, Works and Days 80-82)

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *deh₃- 'to give' — the root of δῶρον, Latin dōnum, English 'donor' and 'donation'

kin.label: Family
kin.form: Wife of Epimētheus, daughter-in-law of Promētheus — the jar she carries becomes the myth's engine (Apollodorus, Library 1.7.2)

pronunciation.note: Pandōra is Tier 1: the Greek Πανδώρα carries both the acute stress and a genuinely long omega, the two features the ASCII 'pandora' flattens completely.

domains.title: First Woman
domains.subtitle: First Woman and the Jar of Evils
domains.lead: Pandōra is the woman the gods made as punishment: shaped from earth and water, dressed by Athēnâ, filled with longing by Aphrodítē, and sent to Epimētheus with a jar that holds every sorrow mortal life would ever know. Her name means 'All-gifted' — because every Olympian gave her something.

cards.name: The Fashioning
cards.desc: Hephaistos mixed earth and water into a 'beautiful evil'; Athēnâ dressed her and taught her weaving (Hesiod, Theogony 570-584; Works and Days 60-68).

cards.name: All-Gifted
cards.desc: Aphrodítē poured in grace and cruel longing, Hermēs a lying tongue and a thievish heart — 'because all the Olympians gave her a gift, a bane to men' (Works and Days 69-82).

cards.name: The Jar of Evils
cards.desc: Not a box: a pithos, a great storage-jar, whose lifted lid releases toil, disease, and old age into the world (Works and Days 90-105).

cards.name: Hope Remains
cards.desc: Only Elpis, Hope, stayed under the rim — a mercy, or Zeus's final cruelty; Hesiod leaves it deliberately unclear (Works and Days 96-104).

symbols.name: The storage-jar (pithos)
symbols.meaning: The great earthenware vessel from which every mortal ill escaped — a household jar, which is precisely Hesiod's point: evil enters the world through the home

symbols.name: The lid
symbols.meaning: Her hand on the rim is the most reproduced gesture in the tradition; the myth turns on a single motion that cannot be reversed

symbols.name: Elpis (Hope)
symbols.meaning: The one presence left inside the jar — read by ancient and modern readers alike both as the last mercy and as the gods' final bait

symbols.name: Clay
symbols.meaning: She was kneaded from earth and water by Hephaistos — a divine artifact built of human material

symbols.name: The floral crown
symbols.meaning: The Horae crowned her with spring flowers, and Athēnâ veiled her — beauty as the wrapping of the trap (Works and Days 72-76)

symbols.name: The girdle
symbols.meaning: Aphrodítē's contribution of longing and care — desire sewn into the gift so that it cannot be refused

mythology.lead: Pandōra's story is told almost entirely by Hesiod, twice — in the Theogony and the Works and Days — and it is the Greek myth of myth-making itself: how the gods answered fire with a counter-gift, and how a name can mean blessing and bane at once. Later ages added the box; Hesiod's jar is the original.

myths.title: A Beautiful Evil, Built by Committee
myths.text: After Promētheus stole fire, Zeus ordered Hephaistos to 'mix earth with water, and to put in it the voice and strength of humankind,' shaping 'a beautiful evil' in the likeness of a modest maiden (Hesiod, Theogony 570-584). The gods then worked her over like a dedication: Athēnâ dressed her in silver-white robes and set a veil on her head; the Horae crowned her with spring flowers; Aphrodítē 'shed grace upon her head and cruel longing and cares that weary the limbs'; Hermēs gave her 'a bitch's mind and a thievish character' and the gift of winning speech (Works and Days 60-80). Nothing in her is her own — she is a composite artifact, each Olympian's contribution a function. The myth makes the first woman a manufactured object, which is exactly the bitterness Hesiod wants us to taste: Pandōra is a tool disguised as a bride.

myths.title: Sent to Epimētheus
myths.text: Zeus named her Pandōra — 'because all the Olympians gave her a gift, a bane to industrious men' (Hesiod, Works and Days 80-82) — and had Hermēs take her to earth with a great storage-jar. Promētheus had already warned his brother Epimētheus never to accept a gift from Olympian Zeus; the Works and Days compresses the tragedy into a single line: Epimētheus 'took the evil, and only when he had it perceived the evil' (Op. 88-89). Apollodorus (Library 1.7.2) retells the same scene. The whole machinery of the myth depends on this one moment of ignored foresight: forethought is chained in the Caucasus, afterthought answers the door. From her, Hesiod adds in the Theogony (590-612), descends 'the race of women' — a passage later Greeks found as uncomfortable as we do.

myths.title: All the Evils Take Wing
myths.text: Hesiod continues with terrible speed (Works and Days 90-105): 'the woman took off the great lid of the jar with her hands and scattered all these evils, bringing sorry troubles upon mortals. Only Hope remained there, inside, in the unbreakable home, under the lip of the jar, and did not fly out.' Before this, men lived 'free from ills... without the evil diseases that bring death'; now the jar's winged sorrows fill sea and land — 'for the earth is full of evils, and the sea is full.' Hope stayed, Hesiod adds in a dark aside, 'by the plans of aegis-bearing Zeus,' leaving every reader to decide whether hope is the one mercy left to mortals or the final bait sealed in with them. The vessel, again, was a pithos — a household storage jar; the tradition's later 'box' is Erasmus' sixteenth-century mistranslation, not Hesiod's.

myths.title: All-Gifted, or All-Giving?
myths.text: Already in antiquity the name was argued over. Hesiod glosses it one way — 'all-gifted,' pan-dōra, because every god gave her a gift (Theogony 590; Works and Days 81) — but the same formation can mean 'all-giving,' she from whom all gifts flow, and some ancient readers heard an earth-mother's title beneath it. The Hesiodic Catalogue of Women (fr. 5 M-W) knows a second Pandōra entirely: a daughter of Deukalíōn who bore Graecus to Zeus, ancestress of the Greeks rather than their punishment. Modern scholarship (West, ad Op. 80) notes that both readings are grammatically live. The ambiguity is the myth in miniature: the same figure who pours out every evil also — through the children of her line — becomes the mother of everyone who came after. Her name cannot decide whether she is the vessel of ruin or the source of all that followed.

lore.syncretism: The Romans had no native equivalent and simply kept her Greek name; Hyginus (Fabulae 142) condenses Hesiod for handbook readers, and Ovid passes over her fashioning in silence while retelling the flood around her in-laws. Her great metamorphosis is philological: in 1508 Erasmus, rendering a proverb about ill-considered gifts, translated Hesiod's pithos — a storage-jar — as pyxis, a box, and 'Pandora's box' entered every European language. The Renaissance and Romantic eras remade her as the tragic first woman; Rossetti painted her as a burning-haired femme fatale; modern feminist and psychoanalytic rereading has reclaimed her as the scapegoat of a male poet's misogyny — a reading the text half-invites, since the gods, not she, built the jar and its contents.
lore.culturalLegacy: 'To open Pandora's box' is among the most durable idioms in English and the European languages — for any act that releases consequences no one can recall. The name branded a global jewelry house, a moon of Saturn, and countless works of science fiction; her jar launched the forbidden-container trope that runs from Eden's tree to Bluebeard's chamber. In myth scholarship she remains the case study of how a didactic fable about work and women became the West's default image of unintended consequence. Restoring Pandōra — stress and long omega — restores the name as Hesiod's audience heard it: 'All-gifted,' a phrase that has never stopped meaning two things at once.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Pandōra is a story about storytelling. Hesiod, a didactic poet singing to farmers, needed a reason the world demands labor, and he built it from a name: 'all-gifted.' Everything the gods each contributed, she is a bundle of divine functions wearing a bridal veil. It is one of the most misogynistic passages in Greek literature — and one of the most analyzed, because the cruelty is so visibly constructed. Pandōra did not choose to open the jar in any version Hesiod tells with blame; the evils simply fly, and hope simply stays, and the poet leaves both facts standing.

What she means beyond the dictionary is this: every culture narrates its troubles into being, and the vessel of those troubles always turns out to be someone who had no part in making them. To read her carefully is to unmake the scapegoat and see, instead, the hands that built the jar.

sources.name: Hesiod, Catalogue of Women fr. 5 M-W (the second Pandōra)
Erasmus, Adagia (1508) — source of the 'box' mistranslation; West, Hesiod: Works and Days, ad 80-105

lore.archaeology: No sanctuary of Pandōra is known; her archaeology is iconographic and Attic. White-ground lekythoi of ca. 470-450 BCE — fine funerary oil-flasks — show her emergence from the earth with Hephaistos standing by, hammer still raised, a motif unique to Athens and plausibly tied to the contemporary stage. Later red-figure vases show her simply as a bride, which is Hesiod's bitter point made visible: the gods' punishment arrives wearing wedding clothes. The imagery dies with the classical period and returns only in Renaissance and Romantic painting, where she is reborn as the tragic first woman.
